newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Dutch securities exchanges merge to take on Europe.
newsitem.headline: Dutch securities exchanges merge to take on Europe.

text.p: Amsterdam's stock and options exchanges said on Tuesday they will merge on January 1 next year in a move aimed at bolstering Amsterdam's position in a borderless European capital market after the advent of EMU.

"We aim to remain the chief market for Dutch securities but also to become a major regional player," incoming chief executive of the new organisation, Amsterdam Exchanges (AEX), George Moeller told a news conference.
Members of the Amsterdam Stock Exchange Association approved the merger on Monday night, after it was voted through by members of the European Options Exchange Association last week.

Under the terms of the merger the combined exchange will become a privatised company. The associations of bank and broker members which currently run the respective exchanges will be dismantled in the course of next year.

Moeller said the AEX would have a starting share capital of 100 million guilders on January 1 1997, of which half would be held by the Amsterdam Stock Exchange Association and half by the EOE Association.
The two would subsequently place half of their shareholdings with their members, while the other half would be placed with institutional investors and Amsterdam-listed companies.

Individual shareholdings will be limited to a maximum of 10 percent, with trade in the shares confined to the original stakeholders -- former exchange members, institutional investors and listed companies -- for the first five years, Moeller said.
The shares will carry a seven percent cumulative preference dividend for the first five years.
In addition the AEX will issue profit-sharing certificates entitling holders to the profits remaining after the dividend pay-out.
These certificates will initially be placed with the associations' members and will be freely tradeable.
Moeller said the privatised structure would make the AEX more commercially effective in the battle for market share in a border-free Europe.
"In the past we have to some extent been protected by national borders, (but) these will fall away on January 1, 1999 (the proposed starting date for Economic and Monetary Union)," he said.
"In addition Dutch listed companies are increasingly held in foreign hands and that could be taken as a precursor to a possible migration of capital flows."
The merger was a strategic move to pre-empt such a shift by creating a more marketing-driven organisation, Moeller said.

The AEX would launch an aggressive marketing drive to raise the international profile of its flagship AEX blue-chip index, refine its order-routing system and further commercialise its clearing and settlement facilities, Moeller said.
"We want to give the AEX index a stronger international profile so that it is seen as an indicator in its own right rather than a reflection of (the French) CAC40 or (German) DAX."
Given Dutch firms' global spread of investment, the AEX was a more internationally oriented indicator and had the potential to function in the same way as Morgan Stanley's index, he added.

AEX already had an edge over its competitors in clearing and settlement and would work to further increase its advantage by offering investors the opportunity to settle all share and derivatives transactions through a single system, he said.
Integration would lead to economies of scale as well as reducing risk.
